lead: A radar sees the echo a target sends back, not its outline. Two objects of the same size can return echoes ten thousand times apart, because the echo depends on shape, aspect angle and wavelength. Radar engineers describe a target by one number, its radar cross section σ: an equivalent area in square metres. It sits in the radar range equation and decides how far away a target can be seen; stealth design is the art of making it small.
prereq: You need the radar range equation from Radar range equation and range performance.

blocks.text: A target intercepts some of the incident power and scatters it in many directions. Replace it by an imaginary area that intercepts the incident power density and reradiates it equally in all directions, sized so that the echo density at the radar matches the real one. That area is σ:

blocks.where: σ is the radar cross section in m²; R is the target range in m; S<sub>i</sub> is the incident power density at the target and S<sub>s</sub> the scattered power density back at the radar, both in W/m². Strictly the limit as R → ∞ is taken, so σ does not depend on range.

blocks.text: σ spans many powers of ten, so it is often given in decibels relative to 1 m²: σ(dBsm) = 10 log<sub>10</sub>(σ / 1 m²). Thus 1 m² is 0 dBsm, 100 m² is 20 dBsm and 0.01 m² is −20 dBsm.
σ is not the shadow area. A flat plate facing the radar has a σ thousands of times its area; a carefully shaped body can have far less than its area.

The metal sphere is the one target whose σ is known exactly at every frequency, and it looks the same from every side. With radius a and wavelength λ, the size is measured by ka = 2πa/λ. The figure shows the exact curve; it has three regions:

items: Rayleigh region, ka ≪ 1 (sphere much smaller than λ): σ = 9πa²(ka)⁴, so σ grows as a⁶ and as 1/λ⁴. Raindrops and insects sit here, which is why a shorter wavelength sees rain far more strongly.

Resonance (Mie) region, ka from about 1 to 10: σ swings above and below πa² as the creeping wave around the back adds to or cancels the front reflection. The highest peak, about 3.65πa², comes near ka = 1.
Optical region, ka above about 10: σ = πa², the projected area, independent of λ.

blocks.text: A flat metal plate seen face-on is the opposite extreme. Every point of it reflects in phase, so the fields add and the power grows as the area squared:

blocks.where: A is the plate area in m²; λ is the wavelength in m. It holds only at normal incidence: a few degrees off, the in-phase sum cancels and σ falls by tens of dB.

blocks.text: A corner reflector is three metal plates at right angles (a trihedral). A ray bounces once off each face and leaves parallel to the way it came, so a large echo comes back over a wide cone of angles. For a triangular trihedral of edge a, σ = 4πa⁴/(3λ²); with a = 0.3 m at 9.4 GHz (λ = 0.0319 m), σ = 33.3 m², larger than the echo of many aircraft, from a frame you can carry. Small boats hoist one so marine radar sees them, and radar test ranges use them as calibration targets.

Real targets are collections of panels, edges, cavities and engine inlets. As the target turns, these add and cancel, so σ swings by 10 to 20 dB over a few degrees. Detection theory treats σ as a random number; the fluctuation models are in Detection in noise.

These are orders of magnitude only; the same target changes by 20 dB between nose-on and broadside. Stealth lowers σ in three ways. Shaping removes flat faces and right angles facing likely radars and hides engine faces behind curved ducts. Radar-absorbing material turns the wave into heat in a lossy layer, but works well only over a band of frequencies and adds weight. Low-band radars, whose wavelength is close to the size of tail fins, push the target into the resonance region where shaping helps least.

examples.question: A flat metal plate of area 1 m² faces an X-band radar at 10 GHz. (a) Find its σ in m² and dBsm. (b) A metal sphere has the same projected area, 1 m². Find its radius, ka and σ. (c) Compare the two echoes.
steps: Sphere: πa² = 1 m² gives a = √(1/π) = 0.564 m.
ka = (2π/0.03) × 0.564 = 209.4 × 0.564 = 118.2, far above 10: optical region, so σ = πa² = 1.0 m² = 0 dBsm.
examples.answer: The plate has σ = 13 963 m² (41.4 dBsm) and the sphere 1.0 m² (0 dBsm). Facing the radar, the plate returns about 14 000 times the sphere's echo from the same projected area.

examples.question: A raindrop is a sphere of radius 1 mm. Find its σ at 3 GHz and at 10 GHz, using the Rayleigh formula σ = 9πa²(ka)⁴, and the ratio of the two.
steps: At 3 GHz: λ = 0.1 m; ka = 2π × 0.001 / 0.1 = 0.0628 ≪ 1, so the Rayleigh formula applies.
Ratio: (10/3)⁴ = 123.5, that is 20.9 dB, exactly the 1/λ⁴ law.
examples.answer: σ = 4.41 × 10⁻¹⁰ m² at 3 GHz and 5.44 × 10⁻⁸ m² at 10 GHz: the X-band radar sees each drop 123 times (20.9 dB) more strongly, which is why rain clutter is a high-band problem.

traps: Reading σ as physical area. "The target is 1 m²" means nothing without the band and the aspect.
Carrying a σ value from one band to another. A 1 m nose is in the resonance region at VHF (λ of a few metres) and in the optical region at X band, with very different σ.
Reading 0 dBsm as zero area. It is 1 m²; −20 dBsm is 0.01 m².
Using σ = 4πA²/λ² off normal incidence. A few degrees away the in-phase sum collapses.
Calling ka = 5 the optical region. The optical formula πa² is reliable only above ka ≈ 10.

quiz.q: Define radar cross section and give its unit.
quiz.a: σ = 4πR²S<sub>s</sub>/S<sub>i</sub> (as R → ∞): the area that, intercepting the incident power density and reradiating it equally in all directions, gives the observed echo density at the radar. Unit m², often given in dBsm.

quiz.q: What is 0 dBsm, and what is 20 dBsm in m²?
quiz.a: 0 dBsm is 1 m²; 20 dBsm is 100 m².

quiz.q: Why does a face-on flat plate have a much larger σ than a sphere of the same projected area?
quiz.a: Every point of the plate reflects in phase toward the radar, so the fields add and the power grows as A², giving 4πA²/λ². The sphere's curved surface sends most of its power in other directions, so σ stays near πa².

quiz.q: A metal sphere of radius 10 cm is seen by a 3 GHz radar. Find ka, the region and the approximate σ.
quiz.a: λ = 0.1 m, ka = 2π × 0.1 / 0.1 = 6.28: the upper resonance region, where σ ripples around πa². The exact curve gives about 1.01πa² here, so σ ≈ π × 0.01 = 0.0314 m² (−15.0 dBsm).

quiz.q: A flat plate of area 0.5 m² faces a 3 GHz radar. Find σ in m² and dBsm.
Find σ of a triangular trihedral corner reflector of edge 0.3 m at 9.4 GHz.
A small drone with parts a few centimetres in size is easily seen by an X-band radar but hardly by a VHF radar. Explain.
quiz.a: At VHF the wavelength is metres, so the drone's parts have ka ≪ 1 and sit in the Rayleigh region, where σ ∝ a⁶/λ⁴ is tiny. At X band (3 cm) the same parts have ka near 1 to 10, in the resonance or optical region, and return far more.

quiz.q: An aircraft gives a strong echo broadside and a weak one nose-on. Give two reasons and one design change that lowers both.
quiz.a: Broadside, the long flat fuselage side and the fins face the radar and add in phase; nose-on, mostly curved surfaces and the small inlets face it. Shaping (tilting surfaces away from likely radars and hiding the engine faces) and absorbing coatings lower the returns at all aspects.

beyond: Real RCS prediction is computational: the method of moments for wires and small bodies, physical optics and shooting-and-bouncing rays for large platforms, and full-wave solvers for cavities such as engine ducts. Stealth combines shaping, absorbing materials and control of the aircraft's own emissions. Bistatic radar, with the receiver away from the transmitter, sees a different σ and can defeat shaping. Search for "RCS prediction physical optics", "Swerling models" and "Jaumann absorber" to go further.

figure.caption: The exact cross section of a metal sphere, divided by πa². Small spheres follow 9(ka)⁴, so the raindrop of the second example is 123 times brighter at 10 GHz than at 3 GHz; near ka = 1 the curve peaks at 3.65; above ka ≈ 10 it settles at πa², where the first example's sphere (ka = 118) sits.

spec.aria: Log-log graph of sphere radar cross section over pi a squared against ka from 0.05 to 20. The curve rises steeply along a dashed 9 ka to the fourth line, peaks at 3.65 near ka equals 1, ripples in the shaded resonance band from 1 to 10 and settles at 1 in the optical region. Two points mark a 1 mm raindrop at 3 and 10 GHz.
